## II. Künneth, nonproper supports and the Lefschetz programme

“Il semble que pour les courbes, on récupère … (sans résolution des singularités) … $\rightsquigarrow$ rationalité des fonctions $L$” is a proposed application of the formalism, not a proved curve theorem on this page. A proof would have to identify the extension-by-zero or immersion argument, justify the local terms for the singular coefficient sheaf, and then pass from the trace identities to the Euler product/determinant identity. The finished SGA 5 provides distinct comparison destinations for Lefschetz and for rationality, but the present evidence does not identify this draft with a particular circulated version (Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III; Illusie, 1977, volume contents).
### N21. Formalism is deliberately prioritized over applications

The insertion “th. de bidualité (= dualité locale)” and the sentence “je préfère en compléter les lignes essentielles” locate the author's next work within a chosen formal programme rather than an exhausted list of applications. The juxtaposition of Lefschetz–Cartier and rationality is a research lead, but the overlapping cancellations prevent a confident reconstruction of every proposed transition. This adds manuscript evidence for the README's SGA 4/5 placement while differing in subject from the Hodge-index use of “Lefschetz” in **WG H9**.

“Il ne serait pas admissible de se limiter à des corps” makes the arithmetic objective explicit: the author wants information finer than the fixed-point count modulo $\ell$. The obstruction is that cohomology modules over $\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z$ need not be free, so the usual degreewise finite-projective trace cannot simply be applied to each of them. The subsequent Bourbaki/$\ell$-adic discussion is a workaround under consideration, whereas 128–136 introduces a finite-level complex-theoretic construction; neither passage is a withdrawal of the demand for integral information.
### N24. The finite-level-to-adic passage is an expectation

“On a envie de dire … conséquence formelle, par passage à la limite” proposes deriving the adic formula from finite-level trace identities. To make that claim precise one needs compatible coefficient reduction, an appropriate inverse-limit formalism and control of finiteness; the draft supplies no full inverse-limit argument here. The supplied results register has no entry settling this passage, and the clipped upper addition cannot be used to infer a stronger integrality assertion than the legible text supports.

The words “d'additivité pour un mapping cylindre” should be read with their chain-level compatibility data, not promoted to additivity for every endomorphism of an abstract distinguished triangle. The latter statement is false even for perfect complexes: The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 087L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/087L), Lemma 110.65.1) gives a counterexample. This is a boundary for a possible modern reconstruction, not a contradiction of what the manuscript actually states.

The paragraph beginning “Cet accouplement est induit par un accouplement de nature locale” is cancelled on 144, including the doubtful parenthesis “[pas besoin] que $f$ et $g$ soient propres.” Scan 146 restarts with a trace map and cyclic pairings for pseudo-coherent finite-Tor-dimensional complexes, but the two pages do not finish the entire local-to-global Lefschetz–Verdier theorem. This adds evidence of a change in exposition and should not be recorded as a proved rejection of local pairings or as a completed theorem without properness (compare Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III, §4).
### N41. The stronger trace formalism is a comparison target, not a dating proof

The extension of the formulas of §3.2 to relative divisors is said to hold “de façon évidente,” but its definition depends on the unseen sheaf $\underline R_{X/S}$ from §10.1 and on flatness and local finite presentation of $X/S$. A proof or comparison must first recover that relative meromorphic-function sheaf and the precise meaning of transversality; substituting an arbitrary modern definition of relative Cartier divisor would beg the question. This reused French sheet adds a separate source strand and does not establish a link to **WG H9** merely because both concern divisors or Lefschetz-related geometry.

“La démonstration … sera donnée dans un instant,” the references to unseen axioms (A)/(A'), and the blanks after “EGA IV” make this sheet an incomplete portion of a separate exposition. Its Lemma 5 states the étale-and-radiciel characterization of open immersions, but the preceding theorem and its promised proof cannot be reconstructed from the single page. This adds a source-identification and dependency task, not a basis for filling the bibliographical blanks or attributing the source's every sentence to the handwritten author.

“Tout Module $F$ … est quotient d'un plat” is used to construct bounded-above flat resolutions, and the insertion “ça passe au quotient par quasi-isomorphisme” supplies the key descent assertion for derived tensor. A full proof must control acyclic flat complexes under tensoring and the comparison of resolutions; the manuscript gives the generators $A_U$ but does not write out those verifications here. The modern construction by K-flat resolutions supplies the corresponding framework (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., §21.17–18, [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV)); this comparison restates the mathematical mechanism without importing modern notation into the transcription.

The marginal question “est-ce vrai dans le contexte des topos généraux ?” is attached to the paragraph asserting preservation of flat modules and the resulting tensor comparison, so its scope should remain local to that argument. For morphisms of ringed topoi, the modern derived-pullback construction preserves suitable K-flat resolutions and commutes with derived tensor (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV), Lemmas 21.18.1–4). This confirms a precise modern formulation of the question rather than establishing which axioms the undated draft intended by “topos généraux.”
### N04. Nonflat base change is a later extension

“Remarque sur changement de base non plat” replaces the earlier flatness restriction by a derived pullback defined through flat resolutions, followed on 106 by transitivity “sans hypothèse sur $f,g$ composables.” Relative to 102, this adds a broader construction; it does not retract the flat special case or license replacing every visible $f^*$ by $\mathbb Lf^*$. The modern comparison is the monoidal and compositional structure in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV), Lemmas 21.18.3–4).

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

“C'est peut-être vrai dès que $Y$ est noethérien” concerns finite **relative** cohomological dimension of $f_*$, in the surrounding finite-type discussion, rather than finite absolute cohomological dimension of $Y$. The finite-type-over-a-field case has a direct modern counterpart (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)), and Illusie (2014, Exposé XVIII_A, Corollary 1.4) proves the relative $\ell$-torsion statement for finite-dimensional noetherian $Y$ with $\ell$ invertible on $Y$. Those results confirm qualified versions; these notes leave the draft's full “merely noetherian” scope unresolved and do not offer the absolute cohomology of a field as a counterexample to it.

A concrete check of “même si $X$ … un pt géométrique” is $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and $M=A/\ell A$: the resolution with every differential multiplication by $\ell$ is exact, while tensoring it with $M$ makes every differential zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(M,M)\cong M$ for every $i\geq0$, so locally constant finite modules do not automatically give bounded derived tensor products. This is our elementary example, adding an explicit witness to the manuscript's warning, not a claim that the example is written there.
**Confidence:** high — exactness and the tensor calculation are checked directly.

“Il faut vérifier que c'est un hom fonctoriel pour les catégories dérivées” explicitly leaves a verification after constructing the comparison on resolutions. The subsequent reductions to degree-zero terms and an étale generator, and the marginal proposal to use proper base change on geometric fibres, address why the comparison should be an isomorphism but do not themselves supply every naturality and resolution-independence diagram. This adds a precise unfinished compatibility problem to the README's S19 comparison programme.

“Je pense qu'on doit encore avoir la formule … si $n$ est premier à la caractéristique” asserts the nonproper ordinary-cohomology expectation and proposes local duality as a route. A modern precise statement is The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 0F1P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1P), Lemma 59.97.9): both schemes may be nonproper, provided they are finite type over a separably closed field and $n$ is invertible. This confirms the assertion in that scope, while neither the manuscript nor that modern comparison establishes priority for the proposed proof method.

“Une démonstration presque immédiate” reduces the locally constant-cohomology variant to $M=A_Y$, but the paragraph stops at “où” and does not display the whole dévissage. A secure overlapping theorem is projection for a perfect target complex over any morphism of ringed topoi (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0944](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0944)); this does not by itself settle the manuscript's broader finite-cohomological-dimension/locally-constant variant over a nonregular finite ring. In particular, the finite module in N10 is locally constant at a point and pseudo-coherent there, yet not perfect, so these hypotheses must not be conflated.

“Il semble que pour les courbes, on récupère … (sans résolution des singularités) … $\rightsquigarrow$ rationalité des fonctions $L$” is a proposed application of the formalism, not a proved curve theorem on this page. A proof would have to identify the extension-by-zero or immersion argument, justify the local terms for the singular coefficient sheaf, and then pass from the trace identities to the Euler product/determinant identity. The finished SGA 5 provides distinct comparison destinations for Lefschetz and for rationality, but the present evidence does not identify this draft with a particular circulated version (Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III; Illusie, 1977, volume contents).

The page identifies the intersection of pseudo-coherence and finite Tor dimension with complexes “projectifs de type fini” in finitely many degrees, without introducing the later label “perfect” into its text. Over a ring this is precisely the modern criterion, including control of the representative by a prescribed Tor-amplitude (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0656](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0656), Lemma 15.76.2). The assertion is supplied here as a tool rather than proved in detail, so the draft-to-print comparison should follow the truncation step where the last finitely presented flat module becomes projective.

The phrase “comme une ‘contraction’ au sens tensoriel” turns the degreewise trace into a pairing involving $L^\vee$, biduality and the derived Hom–tensor identification. The modern perfect-duality statement reproduces this mechanism for ringed sites (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0FPP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FPP), Lemma 21.48.4), while the manuscript itself uses it to recover cyclicity and the supertrace formula. This adds a categorical explanation of the construction rather than requiring free cohomology modules, and the overwritten arguments on 136 remain a separate reading problem.

“Il faut savoir que $\mathbb R\Gamma_X(A_X)$ est bien … de Tor-dim finie” is sharpened by the insertion calling pseudo-coherence known and leaving Tor dimension to the next development. The compact-support proposition on 140–142 supplies the missing type of estimate for $Rf_!$, and gives the needed global-cohomology case when the structural morphism is proper; it is not automatically a proof for every nonproper $R\Gamma$. This distinction is an addition to the context's broad SGA placement and prevents treating the passage to $Rf_!$ as an unnoticed substitution for ordinary cohomology.

The inserted hypothesis “l'Anneau de base soit de torsion” belongs to the proposition, whose proof is described as “Résulte … de Künneth.” For compactifiable $f$ with geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, Deligne (1973, XVII, Corollary 5.2.8.1 and Proposition 5.2.9) gives $\mathrm{cd}(Rf_!)\leq2d$ for torsion sheaves and the projection comparison. Our inference sends Tor-amplitude $[a,b]$ in cohomological indexing into $[a,b+2d]$; setting $a=-M,b=-N$ then yields the displayed homological $[N-2d,M]$. This supports the direction of the shift without imposing a prime-to-characteristic hypothesis absent from this compact-support argument.
### N33. The interval letters and the ordinary tensor stay literal

The source alternates $N'$, $M$ and overwritten endpoints, changes the proposition's input from $F_\bullet$ on 140 to $L_\bullet$ on 142, and writes an ordinary tensor on the right of the proof's main formula. The words “notations … de degrés inférieurs” and “notation homologique!” favor a consistent interpretation of the negative shift, but do not decide every overwritten letter or authorize adding a derived decoration to the ordinary tensor. The literature comparison in N32 therefore belongs to the notes, while the different readings and alternatives remain fixed in the LaTeX.

The trace pairing on 144 is qualified by “si $S$ discret” and finite Tor dimension, whereas 146 explicitly requires both finite Tor dimension and pseudo-coherence for its local trace construction. Finite Tor dimension alone cannot supply a finite-projective trace: an infinite-rank free module over a field already has Tor dimension zero, with no ordinary finite-matrix trace of its identity. The intended global setting may inherit constructibility or finiteness assumptions from preceding work, but those assumptions need to be recovered rather than inferred from the insertion alone.

The paragraph beginning “Cet accouplement est induit par un accouplement de nature locale” is cancelled on 144, including the doubtful parenthesis “[pas besoin] que $f$ et $g$ soient propres.” Scan 146 restarts with a trace map and cyclic pairings for pseudo-coherent finite-Tor-dimensional complexes, but the two pages do not finish the entire local-to-global Lefschetz–Verdier theorem. This adds evidence of a change in exposition and should not be recorded as a proved rejection of local pairings or as a completed theorem without properness (compare Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III, §4).

The trace diagram and the final equality with “$\operatorname{sym}$” encode cyclicity through the symmetry of the derived tensor category, so the sign rule is part of the construction and not optional decoration. A proof can use local strictly perfect representatives and then check descent and compatibility of evaluation/coevaluation; the ringed-site duality formulation provides this framework (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0FPP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FPP)). The displayed supertrace and the two composition expressions are written here, but the page stops before a full verification of their compatibility.

The progression from pseudo-coherence and Tor dimension to contraction, then to a sheaf-level trace, is closely aligned with the later organization of perfect-complex theory. SGA 6, Exposé I, §8 is a useful locator for a future facsimile collation, while the independently verified Stacks comparisons used above establish the relevant mathematical statements. This adds a concrete target to **S19** in `README.md`, without claiming that these undated sheets are the text of that exposé or that their relative chronology has been established.

The typed question “under what circumstances this number is an integer” is followed within the reversed printed-page sequence by finite-homological-dimension criteria, residue-extension arguments, and the decomposition theorem. It should therefore be indexed as a question with partial answers in the same reused source, not attributed automatically to the handwritten author's own open programme. The convention on 111 that a local algebra is a localization of a finite algebra is essential when comparing those assertions; the source's full identity and bibliography are not supplied by the context.

A proof or comparison must first recover that relative meromorphic-function sheaf and the precise meaning of transversality; substituting an arbitrary modern definition of relative Cartier divisor would beg the question. This reused French sheet adds a separate source strand and does not establish a link to **WG H9** merely because both concern divisors or Lefschetz-related geometry.

The assertion that the normalization of a one-dimensional local domain is a semilocal PID is correct under the usual Noetherian convention: normalization is semilocal Dedekind, and its invertible ideals are principal (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tags 09IG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09IG), [09N2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09N2), [02M9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02M9)). Thus absence of module-finite normalization or excellence is not by itself a gap in this lemma. What remains to recover is the reused source's convention for “local domain,” which is not spelled out in the surviving statement; a non-Noetherian reading would be a materially different claim.

The separate implication “same characteristic so that $R$ has a coefficient field” also needs qualification: $\mathbb Q[x,y]_{(x^2-2,y)}$ is equicharacteristic regular local of dimension two with residue field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, but its fraction field $\mathbb Q(x,y)$ contains no square root of $2$. Thus no coefficient field can map isomorphically to that residue field, while the complete-local Cohen theorem provides one in its own hypotheses (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 032A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032A)). This is our second conditional scope test, distinct from N50, not an assertion that the unseen preceding hypotheses were absent.

The definition of an immediate quadratic transform localizes $R[Mx^{-1}]$ at a **maximal** ideal, and Lemma 9 then changes a chart basis while preserving the specified local ring. This matters for any attempted comparison with all points of a blowup, since the generic points of exceptional divisors are not covered by the same dimension assertion without changing the formulation. The package adds a source-specific convention; no comparison with resolution or with a register entry should erase the maximal-centre condition.
### N54. The literal étale criterion admits a dual-number counterexample

In condition (c), finite separability of $\kappa(y)/\kappa(x)$ alone does not imply the subsequent equality $m_y=m_xO_y$: $\operatorname{Spec}(k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2)\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite, flat and finitely presented, with residue extension $k/k$, but has $m_y=(\varepsilon)\ne0$. Its nonreduced fibre prevents étaleness, in agreement with the criterion requiring étale fibres (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03PC](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03PC), Proposition 59.26.2). This is a counterexample to the isolated residue-field-only wording as transcribed, not to the stronger condition printed immediately afterward or to an unseen theorem elsewhere.

matches.excerpt: ### N02. Flat resolutions and the quotient by quasi-isomorphisms

“Tout Module $F$ … est quotient d'un plat” is used to construct bounded-above flat resolutions, and the insertion “ça passe au quotient par quasi-isomorphisme” supplies the key descent assertion for derived tensor. A full proof must control acyclic flat complexes under tensoring and the comparison of resolutions; the manuscript gives the generators $A_U$ but does not write out those verifications here. The modern construction by K-flat resolutions supplies the corresponding framework (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., §21.17–18, [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV)); this comparison restates the mathematical mechanism without importing modern notation into the transcription.

“Remarque sur changement de base non plat” replaces the earlier flatness restriction by a derived pullback defined through flat resolutions, followed on 106 by transitivity “sans hypothèse sur $f,g$ composables.” Relative to 102, this adds a broader construction; it does not retract the flat special case or license replacing every visible $f^*$ by $\mathbb Lf^*$. The modern comparison is the monoidal and compositional structure in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV), Lemmas 21.18.3–4).

The marginal “Mais il faut supposer … que $\Gamma_X$ est de dim … finie !” qualifies the unrestricted global hyper-Tor construction, while another note treats a bounded-below second argument for derived internal Hom. These qualifications add evidence that the author is tracking the distinction between existence in a selected derived-category range and preservation of bounds, rather than simply manipulating formal symbols. The small wording of the first qualification is uncertain, so it should not be used as a fully precise general nonexistence theorem for unbounded derived functors.

The proposed proof of adjunction is qualified by the marginal “Attention, [ne marche que si] $f$ est plat,” followed by a reduction to a generator and a localization diagram. What is withdrawn is the unrestricted use of that injective-resolution argument, not the adjunction statement itself; the replacement argument is sketched rather than fully checked, and its generator decoration is a low-confidence reading. Both the initial argument and its same-page correction therefore belong to the record, with the uncertainty of the marginal wording retained.

The “Formule de projection” on this sheet is the derived internal-Hom comparison, supported by the external-Hom adjunction and the assertion that the localization square permits the needed base change. Its proof obligation is compatibility of those constructions with restriction to the indicated localizations, not an arbitrary base-change theorem for every square. This adds a local-to-global proof strategy to the supplied plan; no corresponding assertion or scan is present in the context register.

“Il faut vérifier que c'est un hom fonctoriel pour les catégories dérivées” explicitly leaves a verification after constructing the comparison on resolutions. The subsequent reductions to degree-zero terms and an étale generator, and the marginal proposal to use proper base change on geometric fibres, address why the comparison should be an isomorphism but do not themselves supply every naturality and resolution-independence diagram. This adds a precise unfinished compatibility problem to the README's S19 comparison programme.
### N14. One proper factor and the characteristic restriction

The manuscript says the ordinary-direct-image analogue would force a vanishing off an open set “ce qui n'est pas vrai si $f$ non propre.” An explicit model is $j:\mathbb G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, with $k$ algebraically closed, $L=\Lambda$ on $\mathbb G_m$ and $M=j_!\Lambda$ for a finite field of coefficients: at a geometric point over $0$, $(Rj_*L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ has zero stalk, whereas $Rj_*(L\otimes j^*M)$ has nonzero $H^0$ stalk. This adds a concrete boundary calculation to the manuscript's mechanism; the connected punctured strict-local neighbourhood gives the nonzero constant section.
**Confidence:** high — the two stalks differ already in degree zero.

The manuscript uses one fixed interval for “tout pt géom,” a quantifier that should be retained in any reconstruction. On a disjoint union of infinitely many points, put a copy of $A$ in cohomological degree $-n$ on the $n$th component: this is locally perfect and bounded above, with finite Tor-amplitude at every stalk, but it has no single global finite amplitude interval. The example distinguishes the manuscript's uniform claim from the local perfectness criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 08G8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08G8)); it does not refute the fixed-interval stalkwise criterion on the page.

The inserted hypothesis “l'Anneau de base soit de torsion” belongs to the proposition, whose proof is described as “Résulte … de Künneth.” For compactifiable $f$ with geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, Deligne (1973, XVII, Corollary 5.2.8.1 and Proposition 5.2.9) gives $\mathrm{cd}(Rf_!)\leq2d$ for torsion sheaves and the projection comparison. Our inference sends Tor-amplitude $[a,b]$ in cohomological indexing into $[a,b+2d]$; setting $a=-M,b=-N$ then yields the displayed homological $[N-2d,M]$. This supports the direction of the shift without imposing a prime-to-characteristic hypothesis absent from this compact-support argument.

The trace diagram and the final equality with “$\operatorname{sym}$” encode cyclicity through the symmetry of the derived tensor category, so the sign rule is part of the construction and not optional decoration. A proof can use local strictly perfect representatives and then check descent and compatibility of evaluation/coevaluation; the ringed-site duality formulation provides this framework (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0FPP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FPP)). The displayed supertrace and the two composition expressions are written here, but the page stops before a full verification of their compatibility.

The typed question “under what circumstances this number is an integer” is followed within the reversed printed-page sequence by finite-homological-dimension criteria, residue-extension arguments, and the decomposition theorem. It should therefore be indexed as a question with partial answers in the same reused source, not attributed automatically to the handwritten author's own open programme. The convention on 111 that a local algebra is a localization of a finite algebra is essential when comparing those assertions; the source's full identity and bibliography are not supplied by the context.

The principal handwritten sequence concerns derived operations, projection and Künneth, traces over finite coefficient rings, Tor bounds and the beginning of a Lefschetz–Verdier construction. “C'est peut-être vrai dès que $Y$ est noethérien” concerns finite **relative** cohomological dimension of $f_*$, in the surrounding finite-type discussion, rather than finite absolute cohomological dimension of $Y$. The finite-type-over-a-field case has a direct modern counterpart (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)), and Illusie (2014, Exposé XVIII_A, Corollary 1.4) proves the relative $\ell$-torsion statement for finite-dimensional noetherian $Y$ with $\ell$ invertible on $Y$. Those results confirm qualified versions; these notes leave the draft's full “merely noetherian” scope unresolved and do not offer the absolute cohomology of a field as a counterexample to it.

The inserted hypothesis “l'Anneau de base soit de torsion” belongs to the proposition, whose proof is described as “Résulte … de Künneth.” For compactifiable $f$ with geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, Deligne (1973, XVII, Corollary 5.2.8.1 and Proposition 5.2.9) gives $\mathrm{cd}(Rf_!)\leq2d$ for torsion sheaves and the projection comparison. ### N08. Finite coefficient rings force attention to unbounded resolutions

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

The manuscript says the ordinary-direct-image analogue would force a vanishing off an open set “ce qui n'est pas vrai si $f$ non propre.” An explicit model is $j:\mathbb G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, with $k$ algebraically closed, $L=\Lambda$ on $\mathbb G_m$ and $M=j_!\Lambda$ for a finite field of coefficients: at a geometric point over $0$, $(Rj_*L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ has zero stalk, whereas $Rj_*(L\otimes j^*M)$ has nonzero $H^0$ stalk. This adds a concrete boundary calculation to the manuscript's mechanism; the connected punctured strict-local neighbourhood gives the nonzero constant section.

“Il semble que pour les courbes, on récupère … (sans résolution des singularités) … $\rightsquigarrow$ rationalité des fonctions $L$” is a proposed application of the formalism, not a proved curve theorem on this page. A proof would have to identify the extension-by-zero or immersion argument, justify the local terms for the singular coefficient sheaf, and then pass from the trace identities to the Euler product/determinant identity. The finished SGA 5 provides distinct comparison destinations for Lefschetz and for rationality, but the present evidence does not identify this draft with a particular circulated version (Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III; Illusie, 1977, volume contents).

The schematic equality with “nb de pts fixes” is immediately qualified by “avec grain de sel,” and isolated fixed points are said to require suitable multiplicities. The later promise “On donnera l'approche de Verdier” leaves both the general coefficient-sheaf construction and the promised elementary derivation to be developed beyond this opening paragraph. This adds a trace/local-term programme, not a count of fixed points with multiplicity one; comparison with the finished exposition belongs at Grothendieck (1977, Exposé III, §§3–4).

“Il ne serait pas admissible de se limiter à des corps” makes the arithmetic objective explicit: the author wants information finer than the fixed-point count modulo $\ell$. The obstruction is that cohomology modules over $\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z$ need not be free, so the usual degreewise finite-projective trace cannot simply be applied to each of them. The subsequent Bourbaki/$\ell$-adic discussion is a workaround under consideration, whereas 128–136 introduces a finite-level complex-theoretic construction; neither passage is a withdrawal of the demand for integral information.

u=\mathbb Z/\ell^
u\mathbb Z$, with endomorphisms and compatible derived coefficient reduction. Degreewise matrix trace commutes with reduction, so their supertraces form an element of $\varprojlim A_

The typed parenthesis “then $R=k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$” is not a consequence of equal characteristic and a regular system of parameters alone: $R=\mathbb Q[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ is countable and has coefficient field $\mathbb Q$, whereas $\mathbb Q[[x,y]]$ is uncountable. This checks the manuscript's failure claim and is consistent with the doubtful addition “même pour $H^1$,” but it gives no permission to remove that paleographic doubt from the frozen text.

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

“C'est peut-être vrai dès que $Y$ est noethérien” concerns finite **relative** cohomological dimension of $f_*$, in the surrounding finite-type discussion, rather than finite absolute cohomological dimension of $Y$. The finite-type-over-a-field case has a direct modern counterpart (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)), and Illusie (2014, Exposé XVIII_A, Corollary 1.4) proves the relative $\ell$-torsion statement for finite-dimensional noetherian $Y$ with $\ell$ invertible on $Y$. Those results confirm qualified versions; these notes leave the draft's full “merely noetherian” scope unresolved and do not offer the absolute cohomology of a field as a counterexample to it.

A concrete check of “même si $X$ … un pt géométrique” is $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and $M=A/\ell A$: the resolution with every differential multiplication by $\ell$ is exact, while tensoring it with $M$ makes every differential zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(M,M)\cong M$ for every $i\geq0$, so locally constant finite modules do not automatically give bounded derived tensor products. This is our elementary example, adding an explicit witness to the manuscript's warning, not a claim that the example is written there.

## III. Traces over finite rings and perfect complexes
### N23. Why reduction to a finite field is rejected

“Il ne serait pas admissible de se limiter à des corps” makes the arithmetic objective explicit: the author wants information finer than the fixed-point count modulo $\ell$. The obstruction is that cohomology modules over $\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z$ need not be free, so the usual degreewise finite-projective trace cannot simply be applied to each of them. The subsequent Bourbaki/$\ell$-adic discussion is a workaround under consideration, whereas 128–136 introduces a finite-level complex-theoretic construction; neither passage is a withdrawal of the demand for integral information.
### N24. The finite-level-to-adic passage is an expectation

“On a envie de dire … conséquence formelle, par passage à la limite” proposes deriving the adic formula from finite-level trace identities. The marginal “Mais il faut supposer … que $\Gamma_X$ est de dim … finie !” qualifies the unrestricted global hyper-Tor construction, while another note treats a bounded-below second argument for derived internal Hom. These qualifications add evidence that the author is tracking the distinction between existence in a selected derived-category range and preservation of bounds, rather than simply manipulating formal symbols. The small wording of the first qualification is uncertain, so it should not be used as a fully precise general nonexistence theorem for unbounded derived functors.

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

“Il faut vérifier que c'est un hom fonctoriel pour les catégories dérivées” explicitly leaves a verification after constructing the comparison on resolutions. The subsequent reductions to degree-zero terms and an étale generator, and the marginal proposal to use proper base change on geometric fibres, address why the comparison should be an isomorphism but do not themselves supply every naturality and resolution-independence diagram. ### N16. An explicit characteristic-p failure in degree one

For algebraically closed $k$ of characteristic $p$, Artin–Schreier gives $H^1_{\mathrm{ét}}(\mathbb A_k^2,\mathbb F_p)=k[x,y]/\{h^p-h\}$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0A3J](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3J)). The class of $xy$ does not come from the sum of the two one-variable cohomology groups: an equality $xy=a(x)+b(y)+h^p-h$ would leave, after discarding pure-variable monomials, a mixed polynomial $q$ with $q^p-q=xy$, which is impossible by its highest total degree. This checks the manuscript's failure claim and is consistent with the doubtful addition “même pour $H^1$,” but it gives no permission to remove that paleographic doubt from the frozen text.

The manuscript says the ordinary-direct-image analogue would force a vanishing off an open set “ce qui n'est pas vrai si $f$ non propre.” An explicit model is $j:\mathbb G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, with $k$ algebraically closed, $L=\Lambda$ on $\mathbb G_m$ and $M=j_!\Lambda$ for a finite field of coefficients: at a geometric point over $0$, $(Rj_*L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ has zero stalk, whereas $Rj_*(L\otimes j^*M)$ has nonzero $H^0$ stalk. Let $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and take the two-term complex $P=[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ in degrees $0,1$. It is perfect, with $H^0(P)\cong H^1(P)\cong A/\ell A$ nonprojective, while the trace of its identity is unambiguously $1-1=0$ in $A$ by the finite-projective supertrace formula (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)). It is therefore a proof sketch completed in these pages, not an indefinitely abandoned existence claim. The corresponding independence-of-representative statement is verified in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)); the manuscript's contribution to the supplied plan is its explicit passage from an alternating expression to a derived invariant.

The modern perfect-duality statement reproduces this mechanism for ringed sites (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0FPP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FPP), Lemma 21.48.4), while the manuscript itself uses it to recover cyclicity and the supertrace formula. ## IV. Tor bounds and cohomological correspondences
### N31. Uniform Tor bounds versus pointwise finite bounds

The manuscript uses one fixed interval for “tout pt géom,” a quantifier that should be retained in any reconstruction. On a disjoint union of infinitely many points, put a copy of $A$ in cohomological degree $-n$ on the $n$th component: this is locally perfect and bounded above, with finite Tor-amplitude at every stalk, but it has no single global finite amplitude interval. The example distinguishes the manuscript's uniform claim from the local perfectness criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 08G8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08G8)); it does not refute the fixed-interval stalkwise criterion on the page.

In the inserted phrase “loc. libre de t.f., et borné,” the words “et borné” are themselves deleted, so they cannot be treated as a surviving hypothesis on this page. An infinite direct sum of contractible two-term free complexes placed in disjoint, successively negative degrees represents the zero, hence perfect, derived object, yet its identity has no finite degreewise alternating sum on that unbounded representative. Thus the literal representative-based formula needs local bounded representatives or another specified interpretation; this is a conditional scope objection, not a reason to restore the deletion or deny the intrinsic trace of the perfect object.

A useful next check would ask whether the normalized multiplicity calculation factors through an appropriate $K_0$ class before any trace interpretation is asserted. Lemma 6 says the preservation of tame ramification “Follows from Lemmas 6 and 7 of Part I and [A7, Proposition 1.50 of Section 7].” Those references and the definition of tameness must be recovered before the statement is used beyond the typed normal projective setting, and the visible $K^*$/$K'$ discrepancy remains a reading question. ### N49. Normalization does not need to be finite as a module

The assertion that the normalization of a one-dimensional local domain is a semilocal PID is correct under the usual Noetherian convention: normalization is semilocal Dedekind, and its invertible ideals are principal (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tags 09IG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09IG), [09N2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09N2), [02M9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02M9)). Its proof obligation is compatibility of those constructions with restriction to the indicated localizations, not an arbitrary base-change theorem for every square. ### N11. Compact-support projection and the literal formulas
## II. Künneth, nonproper supports and the Lefschetz programme

“S'obtient en appliquant 2 fois la formule de projection” compresses the compact-support Künneth proof, and the margin records that projection is recovered by specializing one structural morphism to an isomorphism. The page also rewrites its flatness assumptions, so the flat-sheaf special case should be distinguished from the derived statement and from a formula without Tor contributions. Deligne (1973, XVII, Theorem 5.4.3) is a published comparison locator for the compact-support result; identity of the canonical comparison maps remains part of the draft-to-print study.

The argument beginning “si $X$ ou $Y$ propre sur $k$” combines proper base change with projection and is explicitly distinguished on 120 from statements requiring $n$ prime to the characteristic. The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 0F14](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F14), Lemma 59.97.2(2)) confirms this one-proper-factor formula for finite-type schemes over a separably closed field and arbitrary $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ complexes, without assuming $n$ invertible. This comparison supports the manuscript's distinction rather than transferring the later prime-to-characteristic condition backwards to all Künneth formulas in the package.

“Je pense qu'on doit encore avoir la formule … si $n$ est premier à la caractéristique” asserts the nonproper ordinary-cohomology expectation and proposes local duality as a route. This confirms the assertion in that scope, while neither the manuscript nor that modern comparison establishes priority for the proposed proof method.

The manuscript says the ordinary-direct-image analogue would force a vanishing off an open set “ce qui n'est pas vrai si $f$ non propre.” An explicit model is $j:\mathbb G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, with $k$ algebraically closed, $L=\Lambda$ on $\mathbb G_m$ and $M=j_!\Lambda$ for a finite field of coefficients: at a geometric point over $0$, $(Rj_*L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ has zero stalk, whereas $Rj_*(L\otimes j^*M)$ has nonzero $H^0$ stalk. This adds a concrete boundary calculation to the manuscript's mechanism; the connected punctured strict-local neighbourhood gives the nonzero constant section.

“On a envie de dire … conséquence formelle, par passage à la limite” proposes deriving the adic formula from finite-level trace identities. To make that claim precise one needs compatible coefficient reduction, an appropriate inverse-limit formalism and control of finiteness; the draft supplies no full inverse-limit argument here. The supplied results register has no entry settling this passage, and the clipped upper addition cannot be used to infer a stronger integrality assertion than the legible text supports.

“Il faut savoir que $\mathbb R\Gamma_X(A_X)$ est bien … de Tor-dim finie” is sharpened by the insertion calling pseudo-coherence known and leaving Tor dimension to the next development. The compact-support proposition on 140–142 supplies the missing type of estimate for $Rf_!$, and gives the needed global-cohomology case when the structural morphism is proper; it is not automatically a proof for every nonproper $R\Gamma$. This distinction is an addition to the context's broad SGA placement and prevents treating the passage to $Rf_!$ as an unnoticed substitution for ordinary cohomology.
### N32. The compact-support amplitude estimate

The inserted hypothesis “l'Anneau de base soit de torsion” belongs to the proposition, whose proof is described as “Résulte … de Künneth.” For compactifiable $f$ with geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, Deligne (1973, XVII, Corollary 5.2.8.1 and Proposition 5.2.9) gives $\mathrm{cd}(Rf_!)\leq2d$ for torsion sheaves and the projection comparison. Our inference sends Tor-amplitude $[a,b]$ in cohomological indexing into $[a,b+2d]$; setting $a=-M,b=-N$ then yields the displayed homological $[N-2d,M]$. This supports the direction of the shift without imposing a prime-to-characteristic hypothesis absent from this compact-support argument.
### N33. The interval letters and the ordinary tensor stay literal

The source alternates $N'$, $M$ and overwritten endpoints, changes the proposition's input from $F_\bullet$ on 140 to $L_\bullet$ on 142, and writes an ordinary tensor on the right of the proof's main formula. The words “notations … de degrés inférieurs” and “notation homologique!” favor a consistent interpretation of the negative shift, but do not decide every overwritten letter or authorize adding a derived decoration to the ordinary tensor. The literature comparison in N32 therefore belongs to the notes, while the different readings and alternatives remain fixed in the LaTeX.

The trace pairing on 144 is qualified by “si $S$ discret” and finite Tor dimension, whereas 146 explicitly requires both finite Tor dimension and pseudo-coherence for its local trace construction. Finite Tor dimension alone cannot supply a finite-projective trace: an infinite-rank free module over a field already has Tor dimension zero, with no ordinary finite-matrix trace of its identity. The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

“C'est peut-être vrai dès que $Y$ est noethérien” concerns finite **relative** cohomological dimension of $f_*$, in the surrounding finite-type discussion, rather than finite absolute cohomological dimension of $Y$. The finite-type-over-a-field case has a direct modern counterpart (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)), and Illusie (2014, Exposé XVIII_A, Corollary 1.4) proves the relative $\ell$-torsion statement for finite-dimensional noetherian $Y$ with $\ell$ invertible on $Y$. Those results confirm qualified versions; these notes leave the draft's full “merely noetherian” scope unresolved and do not offer the absolute cohomology of a field as a counterexample to it.

A concrete check of “même si $X$ … un pt géométrique” is $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and $M=A/\ell A$: the resolution with every differential multiplication by $\ell$ is exact, while tensoring it with $M$ makes every differential zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(M,M)\cong M$ for every $i\geq0$, so locally constant finite modules do not automatically give bounded derived tensor products. This is our elementary example, adding an explicit witness to the manuscript's warning, not a claim that the example is written there.
### N19. The locally constant variant needs its actual scope

“Une démonstration presque immédiate” reduces the locally constant-cohomology variant to $M=A_Y$, but the paragraph stops at “où” and does not display the whole dévissage. A secure overlapping theorem is projection for a perfect target complex over any morphism of ringed topoi (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0944](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0944)); this does not by itself settle the manuscript's broader finite-cohomological-dimension/locally-constant variant over a nonregular finite ring. In particular, the finite module in N10 is locally constant at a point and pseudo-coherent there, yet not perfect, so these hypotheses must not be conflated.

Let $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and take the two-term complex $P=[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ in degrees $0,1$. It is perfect, with $H^0(P)\cong H^1(P)\cong A/\ell A$ nonprojective, while the trace of its identity is unambiguously $1-1=0$ in $A$ by the finite-projective supertrace formula (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)). This gives a concrete reason for the manuscript's replacement of the system of cohomology groups by its complex, and differs from N10 because the **object** here is perfect even though its cohomology modules are not.
### N26. The unnamed perfectness criterion

The page identifies the intersection of pseudo-coherence and finite Tor dimension with complexes “projectifs de type fini” in finitely many degrees, without introducing the later label “perfect” into its text. Over a ring this is precisely the modern criterion, including control of the representative by a prescribed Tor-amplitude (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0656](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0656), Lemma 15.76.2). The assertion is supplied here as a tool rather than proved in detail, so the draft-to-print comparison should follow the truncation step where the last finitely presented flat module becomes projective.

“Il faut savoir que $\mathbb R\Gamma_X(A_X)$ est bien … de Tor-dim finie” is sharpened by the insertion calling pseudo-coherence known and leaving Tor dimension to the next development. The compact-support proposition on 140–142 supplies the missing type of estimate for $Rf_!$, and gives the needed global-cohomology case when the structural morphism is proper; it is not automatically a proof for every nonproper $R\Gamma$. This distinction is an addition to the context's broad SGA placement and prevents treating the passage to $Rf_!$ as an unnoticed substitution for ordinary cohomology.
### N31. Uniform Tor bounds versus pointwise finite bounds

The manuscript uses one fixed interval for “tout pt géom,” a quantifier that should be retained in any reconstruction. On a disjoint union of infinitely many points, put a copy of $A$ in cohomological degree $-n$ on the $n$th component: this is locally perfect and bounded above, with finite Tor-amplitude at every stalk, but it has no single global finite amplitude interval. The example distinguishes the manuscript's uniform claim from the local perfectness criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 08G8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08G8)); it does not refute the fixed-interval stalkwise criterion on the page.
**Confidence:** high — the degrees and the failure of a uniform lower bound are explicit.

The inserted hypothesis “l'Anneau de base soit de torsion” belongs to the proposition, whose proof is described as “Résulte … de Künneth.” For compactifiable $f$ with geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, Deligne (1973, XVII, Corollary 5.2.8.1 and Proposition 5.2.9) gives $\mathrm{cd}(Rf_!)\leq2d$ for torsion sheaves and the projection comparison. Our inference sends Tor-amplitude $[a,b]$ in cohomological indexing into $[a,b+2d]$; setting $a=-M,b=-N$ then yields the displayed homological $[N-2d,M]$. This supports the direction of the shift without imposing a prime-to-characteristic hypothesis absent from this compact-support argument.

The trace pairing on 144 is qualified by “si $S$ discret” and finite Tor dimension, whereas 146 explicitly requires both finite Tor dimension and pseudo-coherence for its local trace construction. Finite Tor dimension alone cannot supply a finite-projective trace: an infinite-rank free module over a field already has Tor dimension zero, with no ordinary finite-matrix trace of its identity. The intended global setting may inherit constructibility or finiteness assumptions from preceding work, but those assumptions need to be recovered rather than inferred from the insertion alone.

The paragraph beginning “Cet accouplement est induit par un accouplement de nature locale” is cancelled on 144, including the doubtful parenthesis “[pas besoin] que $f$ et $g$ soient propres.” Scan 146 restarts with a trace map and cyclic pairings for pseudo-coherent finite-Tor-dimensional complexes, but the two pages do not finish the entire local-to-global Lefschetz–Verdier theorem. This adds evidence of a change in exposition and should not be recorded as a proved rejection of local pairings or as a completed theorem without properness (compare Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III, §4).

In the inserted phrase “loc. libre de t.f., et borné,” the words “et borné” are themselves deleted, so they cannot be treated as a surviving hypothesis on this page. An infinite direct sum of contractible two-term free complexes placed in disjoint, successively negative degrees represents the zero, hence perfect, derived object, yet its identity has no finite degreewise alternating sum on that unbounded representative. Thus the literal representative-based formula needs local bounded representatives or another specified interpretation; this is a conditional scope objection, not a reason to restore the deletion or deny the intrinsic trace of the perfect object.

The progression from pseudo-coherence and Tor dimension to contraction, then to a sheaf-level trace, is closely aligned with the later organization of perfect-complex theory. SGA 6, Exposé I, §8 is a useful locator for a future facsimile collation, while the independently verified Stacks comparisons used above establish the relevant mathematical statements. This adds a concrete target to **S19** in `README.md`, without claiming that these undated sheets are the text of that exposé or that their relative chronology has been established.

The typed question “under what circumstances this number is an integer” is followed within the reversed printed-page sequence by finite-homological-dimension criteria, residue-extension arguments, and the decomposition theorem. It should therefore be indexed as a question with partial answers in the same reused source, not attributed automatically to the handwritten author's own open programme. The convention on 111 that a local algebra is a localization of a finite algebra is essential when comparing those assertions; the source's full identity and bibliography are not supplied by the context.

The assertion that the normalization of a one-dimensional local domain is a semilocal PID is correct under the usual Noetherian convention: normalization is semilocal Dedekind, and its invertible ideals are principal (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tags 09IG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09IG), [09N2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09N2), [02M9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02M9)). Thus absence of module-finite normalization or excellence is not by itself a gap in this lemma. What remains to recover is the reused source's convention for “local domain,” which is not spelled out in the surviving statement; a non-Noetherian reading would be a materially different claim.

The separate implication “same characteristic so that $R$ has a coefficient field” also needs qualification: $\mathbb Q[x,y]_{(x^2-2,y)}$ is equicharacteristic regular local of dimension two with residue field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, but its fraction field $\mathbb Q(x,y)$ contains no square root of $2$. Thus no coefficient field can map isomorphically to that residue field, while the complete-local Cohen theorem provides one in its own hypotheses (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 032A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032A)). This is our second conditional scope test, distinct from N50, not an assertion that the unseen preceding hypotheses were absent.

The definition of an immediate quadratic transform localizes $R[Mx^{-1}]$ at a **maximal** ideal, and Lemma 9 then changes a chart basis while preserving the specified local ring. This matters for any attempted comparison with all points of a blowup, since the generic points of exceptional divisors are not covered by the same dimension assertion without changing the formulation. The package adds a source-specific convention; no comparison with resolution or with a register entry should erase the maximal-centre condition.

The principal handwritten sequence concerns derived operations, projection and Künneth, traces over finite coefficient rings, Tor bounds and the beginning of a Lefschetz–Verdier construction. It supports the README's broad SGA 4/5 placement, while the **24 reused typescript pages** also contain operator theory, ramification, relative divisors, local algebra and an axiomatic étale-topos exposition. Those typed sources are not silently assigned to Grothendieck's authorship or treated as his own conjectures.

### N08. Finite coefficient rings force attention to unbounded resolutions

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

The manuscript says the ordinary-direct-image analogue would force a vanishing off an open set “ce qui n'est pas vrai si $f$ non propre.” An explicit model is $j:\mathbb G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, with $k$ algebraically closed, $L=\Lambda$ on $\mathbb G_m$ and $M=j_!\Lambda$ for a finite field of coefficients: at a geometric point over $0$, $(Rj_*L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ has zero stalk, whereas $Rj_*(L\otimes j^*M)$ has nonzero $H^0$ stalk. This adds a concrete boundary calculation to the manuscript's mechanism; the connected punctured strict-local neighbourhood gives the nonzero constant section.
### N20. Curves, singular coefficients and rationality of L-functions

“Il semble que pour les courbes, on récupère … (sans résolution des singularités) … $\rightsquigarrow$ rationalité des fonctions $L$” is a proposed application of the formalism, not a proved curve theorem on this page. A proof would have to identify the extension-by-zero or immersion argument, justify the local terms for the singular coefficient sheaf, and then pass from the trace identities to the Euler product/determinant identity. The finished SGA 5 provides distinct comparison destinations for Lefschetz and for rationality, but the present evidence does not identify this draft with a particular circulated version (Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III; Illusie, 1977, volume contents).

The schematic equality with “nb de pts fixes” is immediately qualified by “avec grain de sel,” and isolated fixed points are said to require suitable multiplicities. The later promise “On donnera l'approche de Verdier” leaves both the general coefficient-sheaf construction and the promised elementary derivation to be developed beyond this opening paragraph. This adds a trace/local-term programme, not a count of fixed points with multiplicity one; comparison with the finished exposition belongs at Grothendieck (1977, Exposé III, §§3–4).

“Il ne serait pas admissible de se limiter à des corps” makes the arithmetic objective explicit: the author wants information finer than the fixed-point count modulo $\ell$. The obstruction is that cohomology modules over $\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z$ need not be free, so the usual degreewise finite-projective trace cannot simply be applied to each of them. The subsequent Bourbaki/$\ell$-adic discussion is a workaround under consideration, whereas 128–136 introduces a finite-level complex-theoretic construction; neither passage is a withdrawal of the demand for integral information.
### N24. The finite-level-to-adic passage is an expectation

“On a envie de dire … conséquence formelle, par passage à la limite” proposes deriving the adic formula from finite-level trace identities. To make that claim precise one needs compatible coefficient reduction, an appropriate inverse-limit formalism and control of finiteness; the draft supplies no full inverse-limit argument here. The supplied results register has no entry settling this passage, and the clipped upper addition cannot be used to infer a stronger integrality assertion than the legible text supports.

On 132, “L'existence … se ramène à prouver” invariance under isomorphism is an unfinished reduction at the page boundary; 134 continues it by vanishing on acyclic bounded finite-projective complexes and short exact sequences. It is therefore a proof sketch completed in these pages, not an indefinitely abandoned existence claim. The corresponding independence-of-representative statement is verified in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)); the manuscript's contribution to the supplied plan is its explicit passage from an alternating expression to a derived invariant.

“Il faut savoir que $\mathbb R\Gamma_X(A_X)$ est bien … de Tor-dim finie” is sharpened by the insertion calling pseudo-coherence known and leaving Tor dimension to the next development. The compact-support proposition on 140–142 supplies the missing type of estimate for $Rf_!$, and gives the needed global-cohomology case when the structural morphism is proper; it is not automatically a proof for every nonproper $R\Gamma$. This distinction is an addition to the context's broad SGA placement and prevents treating the passage to $Rf_!$ as an unnoticed substitution for ordinary cohomology.

The trace pairing on 144 is qualified by “si $S$ discret” and finite Tor dimension, whereas 146 explicitly requires both finite Tor dimension and pseudo-coherence for its local trace construction. Finite Tor dimension alone cannot supply a finite-projective trace: an infinite-rank free module over a field already has Tor dimension zero, with no ordinary finite-matrix trace of its identity. The intended global setting may inherit constructibility or finiteness assumptions from preceding work, but those assumptions need to be recovered rather than inferred from the insertion alone.
### N40. A controlled finite-level compatibility test

A useful intermediate test for the proposed “passage à la limite” is a compatible system of bounded finite-projective complexes over $A_
u=\mathbb Z/\ell^
u\mathbb Z$, with endomorphisms and compatible derived coefficient reduction. Degreewise matrix trace commutes with reduction, so their supertraces form an element of $\varprojlim A_
u=\mathbb Z_\ell$; the additional task is to prove that the geometric cohomology complexes admit the required compatible perfect models. This gives a concrete sufficient mechanism for the manuscript's expectation while leaving that geometric inverse-limit problem open in these pages.
**Confidence:** medium — compatibility of matrix traces is immediate; compatible geometric perfect models have not been proved here.

The typed parenthesis “then $R=k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$” is not a consequence of equal characteristic and a regular system of parameters alone: $R=\mathbb Q[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ is countable and has coefficient field $\mathbb Q$, whereas $\mathbb Q[[x,y]]$ is uncountable. The primary complete-local theorem explicitly assumes completeness (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0C0S](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C0S)). This is a conditional counterexample to the isolated wording, and the right next step is to recover earlier conventions from the reused source before declaring its full theorem false.
### N51. Equal characteristic alone need not give a coefficient field

The separate implication “same characteristic so that $R$ has a coefficient field” also needs qualification: $\mathbb Q[x,y]_{(x^2-2,y)}$ is equicharacteristic regular local of dimension two with residue field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, but its fraction field $\mathbb Q(x,y)$ contains no square root of $2$. Thus no coefficient field can map isomorphically to that residue field, while the complete-local Cohen theorem provides one in its own hypotheses (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 032A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032A)). This is our second conditional scope test, distinct from N50, not an assertion that the unseen preceding hypotheses were absent.

## I. Derived operations and the projection formula
### N01. Exchange identities as a duality programme

The phrase “$D$ ‘échange’” places the immersion calculation within a programme relating direct image, exceptional direct image, pullback and exceptional inverse image through duality. The displayed closed-immersion argument actually gives a calculation using acyclicity and injectivity, so it should not be catalogued as an entirely unsupported assertion merely because the prose calls it “essentiellement trivial.” These pages add a concrete organizational principle to the README's SGA 4/5 mapping request, but the supplied context has no earlier scan against which its first occurrence can be dated.

“Tout Module $F$ … est quotient d'un plat” is used to construct bounded-above flat resolutions, and the insertion “ça passe au quotient par quasi-isomorphisme” supplies the key descent assertion for derived tensor. A full proof must control acyclic flat complexes under tensoring and the comparison of resolutions; the manuscript gives the generators $A_U$ but does not write out those verifications here. The modern construction by K-flat resolutions supplies the corresponding framework (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., §21.17–18, [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV)); this comparison restates the mathematical mechanism without importing modern notation into the transcription.

The marginal question “est-ce vrai dans le contexte des topos généraux ?” is attached to the paragraph asserting preservation of flat modules and the resulting tensor comparison, so its scope should remain local to that argument. For morphisms of ringed topoi, the modern derived-pullback construction preserves suitable K-flat resolutions and commutes with derived tensor (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV), Lemmas 21.18.1–4). This confirms a precise modern formulation of the question rather than establishing which axioms the undated draft intended by “topos généraux.”

“Remarque sur changement de base non plat” replaces the earlier flatness restriction by a derived pullback defined through flat resolutions, followed on 106 by transitivity “sans hypothèse sur $f,g$ composables.” Relative to 102, this adds a broader construction; it does not retract the flat special case or license replacing every visible $f^*$ by $\mathbb Lf^*$. The modern comparison is the monoidal and compositional structure in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV), Lemmas 21.18.3–4).

The marginal “Mais il faut supposer … que $\Gamma_X$ est de dim … finie !” qualifies the unrestricted global hyper-Tor construction, while another note treats a bounded-below second argument for derived internal Hom. These qualifications add evidence that the author is tracking the distinction between existence in a selected derived-category range and preservation of bounds, rather than simply manipulating formal symbols. The small wording of the first qualification is uncertain, so it should not be used as a fully precise general nonexistence theorem for unbounded derived functors.
### N07. Internal-Hom compatibility and its local verification

The “Formule de projection” on this sheet is the derived internal-Hom comparison, supported by the external-Hom adjunction and the assertion that the localization square permits the needed base change. Its proof obligation is compatibility of those constructions with restriction to the indicated localizations, not an arbitrary base-change theorem for every square. This adds a local-to-global proof strategy to the supplied plan; no corresponding assertion or scan is present in the context register.

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

A concrete check of “même si $X$ … un pt géométrique” is $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and $M=A/\ell A$: the resolution with every differential multiplication by $\ell$ is exact, while tensoring it with $M$ makes every differential zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(M,M)\cong M$ for every $i\geq0$, so locally constant finite modules do not automatically give bounded derived tensor products. This is our elementary example, adding an explicit witness to the manuscript's warning, not a claim that the example is written there.

“Il faut vérifier que c'est un hom fonctoriel pour les catégories dérivées” explicitly leaves a verification after constructing the comparison on resolutions. The subsequent reductions to degree-zero terms and an étale generator, and the marginal proposal to use proper base change on geometric fibres, address why the comparison should be an isomorphism but do not themselves supply every naturality and resolution-independence diagram. This adds a precise unfinished compatibility problem to the README's S19 comparison programme.

“S'obtient en appliquant 2 fois la formule de projection” compresses the compact-support Künneth proof, and the margin records that projection is recovered by specializing one structural morphism to an isomorphism. The page also rewrites its flatness assumptions, so the flat-sheaf special case should be distinguished from the derived statement and from a formula without Tor contributions. A modern precise statement is The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 0F1P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1P), Lemma 59.97.9): both schemes may be nonproper, provided they are finite type over a separably closed field and $n$ is invertible. ## III. Traces over finite rings and perfect complexes

The obstruction is that cohomology modules over $\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z$ need not be free, so the usual degreewise finite-projective trace cannot simply be applied to each of them. “On a envie de dire … conséquence formelle, par passage à la limite” proposes deriving the adic formula from finite-level trace identities. To make that claim precise one needs compatible coefficient reduction, an appropriate inverse-limit formalism and control of finiteness; the draft supplies no full inverse-limit argument here. The supplied results register has no entry settling this passage, and the clipped upper addition cannot be used to infer a stronger integrality assertion than the legible text supports.

Let $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and take the two-term complex $P=[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ in degrees $0,1$. It is perfect, with $H^0(P)\cong H^1(P)\cong A/\ell A$ nonprojective, while the trace of its identity is unambiguously $1-1=0$ in $A$ by the finite-projective supertrace formula (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)). This gives a concrete reason for the manuscript's replacement of the system of cohomology groups by its complex, and differs from N10 because the **object** here is perfect even though its cohomology modules are not.
**Confidence:** high — all modules, differential, cohomology and traces are explicit.
### N27. Existence of trace is reduced and then addressed

On 132, “L'existence … se ramène à prouver” invariance under isomorphism is an unfinished reduction at the page boundary; 134 continues it by vanishing on acyclic bounded finite-projective complexes and short exact sequences. It is therefore a proof sketch completed in these pages, not an indefinitely abandoned existence claim. The words “d'additivité pour un mapping cylindre” should be read with their chain-level compatibility data, not promoted to additivity for every endomorphism of an abstract distinguished triangle. The latter statement is false even for perfect complexes: The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 087L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/087L), Lemma 110.65.1) gives a counterexample. This is a boundary for a possible modern reconstruction, not a contradiction of what the manuscript actually states.
### N29. Duality gives the intrinsic trace

The phrase “comme une ‘contraction’ au sens tensoriel” turns the degreewise trace into a pairing involving $L^\vee$, biduality and the derived Hom–tensor identification. This adds a categorical explanation of the construction rather than requiring free cohomology modules, and the overwritten arguments on 136 remain a separate reading problem.

The source alternates $N'$, $M$ and overwritten endpoints, changes the proposition's input from $F_\bullet$ on 140 to $L_\bullet$ on 142, and writes an ordinary tensor on the right of the proof's main formula. The words “notations … de degrés inférieurs” and “notation homologique!” favor a consistent interpretation of the negative shift, but do not decide every overwritten letter or authorize adding a derived decoration to the ordinary tensor. The literature comparison in N32 therefore belongs to the notes, while the different readings and alternatives remain fixed in the LaTeX.

Grothendieck (1977, Exposé III, §§2–3) is a comparison destination for the derived functoriality and correspondence construction, not evidence that the missing characters were present on this sheet.
### N35. The global trace pairing needs a finite object

The trace pairing on 144 is qualified by “si $S$ discret” and finite Tor dimension, whereas 146 explicitly requires both finite Tor dimension and pseudo-coherence for its local trace construction. Finite Tor dimension alone cannot supply a finite-projective trace: an infinite-rank free module over a field already has Tor dimension zero, with no ordinary finite-matrix trace of its identity. This adds evidence of a change in exposition and should not be recorded as a proved rejection of local pairings or as a completed theorem without properness (compare Grothendieck, 1977, Exposé III, §4).
### N37. The local trace and the symmetry sign

The trace diagram and the final equality with “$\operatorname{sym}$” encode cyclicity through the symmetry of the derived tensor category, so the sign rule is part of the construction and not optional decoration. A proof can use local strictly perfect representatives and then check descent and compatibility of evaluation/coevaluation; the ringed-site duality formulation provides this framework (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0FPP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FPP)). The displayed supertrace and the two composition expressions are written here, but the page stops before a full verification of their compatibility.

In the inserted phrase “loc. libre de t.f., et borné,” the words “et borné” are themselves deleted, so they cannot be treated as a surviving hypothesis on this page. An infinite direct sum of contractible two-term free complexes placed in disjoint, successively negative degrees represents the zero, hence perfect, derived object, yet its identity has no finite degreewise alternating sum on that unbounded representative. Thus the literal representative-based formula needs local bounded representatives or another specified interpretation; this is a conditional scope objection, not a reason to restore the deletion or deny the intrinsic trace of the perfect object.

### N13. Künneth is reduced to two projection steps

“S'obtient en appliquant 2 fois la formule de projection” compresses the compact-support Künneth proof, and the margin records that projection is recovered by specializing one structural morphism to an isomorphism. The page also rewrites its flatness assumptions, so the flat-sheaf special case should be distinguished from the derived statement and from a formula without Tor contributions. Deligne (1973, XVII, Theorem 5.4.3) is a published comparison locator for the compact-support result; identity of the canonical comparison maps remains part of the draft-to-print study.

The argument beginning “si $X$ ou $Y$ propre sur $k$” combines proper base change with projection and is explicitly distinguished on 120 from statements requiring $n$ prime to the characteristic. The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 0F14](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F14), Lemma 59.97.2(2)) confirms this one-proper-factor formula for finite-type schemes over a separably closed field and arbitrary $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ complexes, without assuming $n$ invertible. This comparison supports the manuscript's distinction rather than transferring the later prime-to-characteristic condition backwards to all Künneth formulas in the package.

The inserted hypothesis “l'Anneau de base soit de torsion” belongs to the proposition, whose proof is described as “Résulte … de Künneth.” For compactifiable $f$ with geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, Deligne (1973, XVII, Corollary 5.2.8.1 and Proposition 5.2.9) gives $\mathrm{cd}(Rf_!)\leq2d$ for torsion sheaves and the projection comparison.
